title: The Adoration of the Kings
creator: Jan Gossaert (Netherlandish, Maubeuge ca. 1478–1532 Middelburg)
description: This early masterpiece by Jan Gossaert, probably painted shortly after his arrival in Antwerp around 1503, reveals his fascination with the robust figures and detailed realism of fifteenth-century Flemish painting, as well as his interest in the monumental forms and dynamic compositions of Italian Renaissance art. Gossaert’s distinctive style, which combined northern and Italian elements, contributed to the spread of Italian Renaissance ideas in northern Europe.

title: Bust of a Man
creator: Donatello
description: This painted terracotta bust represents a man from the chest up. He wears a tunic with a simple, round neckline. His hair is short and curly, and his expression is serious and contemplative. The bust is attributed to Donatello, a prominent Italian Renaissance sculptor, and is believed to have been created in Florence during the 1450s. The painted surface adds a layer of realism to the sculpture, enhancing the details of the man's features and clothing.

title: The Holy Family with Saint John the Baptist
creator: El Greco (Domenikos Theotokopoulos)
description: A depiction of the Holy Family with Saint John the Baptist, characterized by El Greco's signature elongated figures and dramatic use of light and color.

title: Lovers in an Arbor
creator: Johann Friedrich Lück
description: This painting depicts a courting couple in a lush garden setting. The woman, elegantly dressed, sits on a stone bench within a leafy arbor, while the man stands beside her, gesturing towards a bird perched on a branch. The scene evokes a sense of romantic intimacy and leisure, characteristic of Rococo sensibilities. The artist's attention to detail is evident in the rendering of the foliage, the textures of the clothing, and the delicate expressions of the figures.

title: Model Chalice
creator: Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin
materials: Gilt brass, silver plate, enamel, glass, and semiprecious stones
description: This chalice is a model for a larger liturgical vessel designed by A.W.N. Pugin, the leading architect and designer of the Gothic Revival in England.  Pugin championed the return to medieval forms and craftsmanship, which he believed conveyed greater spiritual truth.  The chalice is richly ornamented with enamels and semiprecious stones, reflecting Pugin's conviction that beauty enhances religious experience.

title: Teapot
creator: Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory; Figures after François Boucher; Painted by Jacques Fontaine
description: This teapot is part of a tea service made by the prestigious Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory.  The figures adorning the teapot were designed by François Boucher, a renowned Rococo artist, and painted by Jacques Fontaine, a skilled painter at the manufactory.  The service exemplifies the elegant and refined style of 18th-century French porcelain.

title: Tray
creator: Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory; Figures after François Boucher; Painted by Jacques Fontaine
description: This exquisite tray, part of a tea service, showcases the renowned craftsmanship of the Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory.  The delicate figures, based on designs by François Boucher, and the vibrant painting by Jacques Fontaine exemplify the rococo style. Crafted from soft-paste porcelain, the tray is adorned with colorful enamels and intricate gilding, adding to its luxurious appeal.

title: Cup and Saucer
creator: Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory; painted by Jacques Fontaine
description: This cup and saucer are part of a tea service made by the prestigious Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory in France.  The delicate floral decoration, attributed to painter Jacques Fontaine, exemplifies the Rococo style popular during the mid-18th century.  While the manufactory was founded in 1740, this particular piece dates to 1763. The vibrant colors and intricate gilding showcase the high level of craftsmanship and artistry for which Sèvres is renowned.

title: Sugar Bowl
creator: Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory; Figures after François Boucher; Painted by Jacques Fontaine
description: This sugar bowl is part of a tea service made by the prestigious Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory in 1763.  The figures adorning the bowl were designed by the renowned Rococo artist François Boucher, and the painting was executed by Jacques Fontaine, a skilled painter at Sèvres.  The delicate floral motifs and gilded details are characteristic of the elegant and luxurious style of Sèvres porcelain during this period. The service reflects the growing popularity of tea drinking in France during the 18th century.

title: Milk Jug
creator: Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory; Figures after François Boucher; Painted by Jacques Fontaine
description: This milk jug is part of a tea service made by the prestigious Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory in 1764.  The figures adorning the jug are based on designs by the renowned Rococo artist François Boucher, and the painting was executed by Jacques Fontaine, a skilled painter at the manufactory.  The delicate floral motifs and gilded details are characteristic of Sèvres porcelain from this period.

title: Ewer and Basin
creator: Capodimonte Porcelain Manufactory, Modeled by Giuseppe Gricci
description: This ewer and basin are examples of Capodimonte porcelain, known for its delicate figures and intricate details.  Modeled by Giuseppe Gricci, a key figure at the Capodimonte factory, the pieces depict scenes of playful putti amidst lush foliage and rocaille ornamentation. The soft pastel colors and lavish gilding are characteristic of the Rococo style prevalent in 18th-century Europe.

title: Christa and Wolfi
creator: Gerhard Richter
description: This double portrait depicts Gerhard Richter's first wife, Christa, and his friend Wolfi.  The blurred effect, achieved by dragging a dry brush across the wet paint, softens the figures and creates a sense of distance, perhaps reflecting the emotional dynamics between the subjects or Richter's own remove from the scene.  The snapshot-like composition and casual poses contribute to the work's informal, intimate feel.

title: Tureen and Stand
creator: Pont-aux-Choux Manufactory
description: This tureen and stand are notable for their vibrant colors and detailed decoration.  The tureen is shaped like a large, plump hen perched atop a nest, with the lid forming the hen's back.  The stand is similarly decorated with flowers, leaves, and insects, creating a cohesive and visually appealing set.  The Pont-aux-Choux Manufactory was known for its innovative and whimsical designs, often incorporating animal and nature motifs into their porcelain wares.

title: Heart Sutra
creator: Yoon Kwang-cho
description: This hanging scroll presents the Heart Sutra, a popular and fundamental text in Mahayana Buddhism.  Written in elegant calligraphy by the contemporary artist Yoon Kwang-cho, the sutra’s message of emptiness and the interconnectedness of all phenomena is enhanced by the artist’s sensitive rendering of the characters.  The fluid brushstrokes and subtle variations in ink tone create a sense of rhythm and movement, inviting contemplation and reflection.

title: Spindle Vase
creator: Lee Young-jae
description: This vase exemplifies the elegant forms and subtle surface decoration characteristic of Lee Young-jae’s work. The artist throws his porcelain vessels on the wheel, often altering their shape by scraping away clay or adding coils. He then applies a coating of white slip, which acts as a ground for his painted decoration. After bisque firing the vase, he paints it with iron oxide and covers it with a transparent glaze. The vase is then reduction fired in a wood-burning kiln, a process that requires constant monitoring of the temperature and oxygen levels. The resulting celadon glaze, with its subtle variations in tone and texture, enhances the quiet beauty of the vase’s form.

title: Berry Dish
creator: Boston & Sandwich Glass Company
description: This blown glass berry dish was made by the Boston & Sandwich Glass Company around 1867.  The company, based in Sandwich, Massachusetts, was known for its pressed and blown glass production during the 19th century. This dish reflects the popular pressed glass patterns of the era.

title: Berry Spoon
creator: J. and W. Moir
description: A silver berry spoon made by J. and W. Moir in New York sometime between 1800 and 1900. It is part of the American Wing collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Betty Lamp
description: This simple, utilitarian lamp, known as a Betty lamp, provided light in American homes from the 17th century until the introduction of glass lamps in the 18th century.  It is made of forged iron and would have burned oil or grease, with a wick extending from the small spout.  Its functional design reflects the needs of early American settlers.

title: Betty Lamp
description: This betty lamp, a simple type of early lighting, is made of iron and dates back to 1725-1775.  It originates from Pennsylvania, in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States.  Betty lamps were common in colonial America and provided a basic source of illumination using a wick and oil or grease. This particular example is part of the American Wing collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Betty Lamp
description: This betty lamp, a simple type of early lighting, is made of iron and dates to 1725–75.  It originates from Pennsylvania, in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States. Betty lamps were common in colonial America, providing a basic source of illumination in homes.

title: Betty Lamp
description: A betty lamp is a simple type of oil lamp, named after the German word *Bette* meaning 'bowl' or 'dish'.  This example, made of wrought iron, would have been a common source of light in homes during the 18th century.  Betty lamps typically consisted of a shallow reservoir for oil, with a small spout or channel to hold a wick. This one has a hook handle, allowing it to be hung on a wall or carried.

title: Betty Lamp
description: A betty lamp is a simple type of oil lamp, named after the German word *Bette* meaning 'bowl' or 'dish'.  This example, made of wrought iron, would have been a common source of light in homes during the 18th century.  A wick, likely made of a twisted piece of fabric, would have been placed in the small reservoir filled with oil, providing a small flame.

title: Bible
creator: George Edward Eyre
description: This 1847 Bible, bound in composition covers, was made by George Edward Eyre and printed by William Spottiswoode in London, England.  It is part of the American Wing collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The Holy Bible: containing the Old Testament and the New
creator: John Hays (Printer)
description: This Bible, printed by John Hays in Cambridge, England in 1674, is a testament to the enduring importance of religious texts in the 17th century.  Bound in leather, this edition reflects the craftsmanship involved in book production during this period.  While the specific edition isn't readily identifiable beyond the printer and date, 17th-century Bibles often featured elaborate title pages, woodcut illustrations, and extensive commentary.  This particular copy resides in the Metropolitan Museum of Art's American Wing, suggesting its relevance to the history of the United States, perhaps brought over by early settlers or reflecting the influence of English printing on the American colonies.

title: Bible
creator: Hodge and Campbell
description: This Bible, published in 1792 by the New York firm of Hodge and Campbell, is part of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's American Wing collection.  It reflects the growing importance of publishing in the newly formed United States.
